# Initialization and Evaluation {#sec-inicializar-evaluar}

<!-- AI translation and naturalness pass: Codex (GPT-6), 2026-10-31. Source: Spanish v1.0, 75b82d8. Preserve the distinction between exact one-step expectations and the deterministic takeover approximation. -->

**Tools:** [initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#lang=en), available through the [portal](https://josemagalan.github.io/genetic-algorithms-lab/#lang=en).

::: {.callout-warning .objetivos title="Chapter Objectives"}
After completing the basic path through this chapter, you will be able to:

- generate individuals in a uniform initial population by hand from given random numbers, including permutations;
- measure population diversity with distances and count feasible individuals;
- recognize when seeding with a heuristic solution may endanger diversity;
- calculate fitness by decoding a chromosome, calculating objective and constraint violation, and penalizing the violation;
- transform a cost into fitness suitable for roulette-wheel selection and calculate the resulting probabilities;
- count evaluations in a run and explain when a cache saves work.
:::

## A Random Population [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme}

A genetic algorithm needs individuals to work on from its first generation. Where do they come from?

A genetic algorithm starts with an **initial population** of *N* individuals, not one solution. Usually these are generated randomly [@talbi2009, p. 194; @mitchell1998, section 1.6]. The initial population need not be good; it needs to be **diverse**, giving selection, crossover, and mutation varied material. Low diversity may cause premature convergence: the algorithm becomes stuck in a region that need not contain the optimum [@talbi2009, p. 193].

**Uniform** means every chromosome has the same probability. For independent genes, sample each separately using a rule appropriate to its type. In each rule, *u* is uniform between 0 and 1:

- **A bit** is 1 if $u < 0.5$, otherwise 0.
- **An integer** from 1 to *m* is $1 + \lfloor u\,m \rfloor$, where $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ denotes the integer part. Each value has probability $1/m$.
- **A real number** in $[a, b]$ is $a + u\,(b - a)$ [@talbi2009, p. 194].

Since genes are sampled independently, every combination has the same probability. The tool displays each random number to two or three decimal places so each gene can be checked by hand.

We use an assignment problem like chapter [](#sec-representacion-entera){.capitulo}, with 5 tasks and 3 machines but different processing times:

| Task | Machine 1 | Machine 2 | Machine 3 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | 5 | 5 | 8 |
| 2 | 9 | 2 | 7 |
| 3 | 2 | 9 | 1 |
| 4 | 7 | 2 | 1 |
| 5 | 3 | 3 | 5 |

The chromosome is an integer vector: gene *i* gives the machine processing task *i*. We minimize **makespan**, the largest machine load. The optimum is 5.

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme title="Reproducible Example · A Random Assignment"}
**Data.** The table's times. For the first individual, numbers $u$ = 0.087, 0.277, 0.454, 0.226, and 0.980 have been drawn, one per task.

**Predict.** Which machine receives each task? What is this individual's makespan?

[Open: the first individual](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&step=7){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

With $m = 3$, each gene is $1 + \lfloor 3u \rfloor$:

| Task | *u* | $3u$ | Machine |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | 0.087 | 0.261 | 1 |
| 2 | 0.277 | 0.831 | 1 |
| 3 | 0.454 | 1.362 | 2 |
| 4 | 0.226 | 0.678 | 1 |
| 5 | 0.980 | 2.940 | 3 |

The individual is **(1, 1, 2, 1, 3)**. Machine 1 processes tasks 1, 2, and 4, giving load $5 + 9 + 7 = 21$; machine 2 processes task 3, load 9; machine 3 processes task 5, load 5. Makespan is **21**, more than four times the optimum.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the tool here (the first individual)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&step=7" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: uniform random, assignment"></iframe>
</details>
:::

The other five individuals are generated the same way with new numbers: their makespans are 9, 8, 14, 14, and 14. None reaches the optimum 5, nor must they: improving the population is the job of the operators that follow.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme title="Exercise · Same Numbers, Different Rules"}
Use the numbers from example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme). (a) Truncate the first five to two decimal places (0.08, 0.27, 0.45, 0.22, 0.98) and generate a 5-bit string. (b) Use the first two, 0.087 and 0.277, to generate a real point in $[-5, 5]^2$. (c) With 4 machines instead of 3, which machine would receive task 5?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) The first four values are below 0.5, but the last is not: **1 1 1 1 0**.

(b) $x_1 = -5 + 0.087 \times 10 = -4.13$ and $x_2 = -5 + 0.277 \times 10 = -2.23$. The point is $(-4.13;\ -2.23)$.

(c) $1 + \lfloor 0.980 \times 4 \rfloor = 1 + \lfloor 3.92 \rfloor = 4$: machine 4.

The randomness is the same; each representation applies a different rule to turn a number into a gene.
</details>
::::

[Explore in initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=assignment-int){.explorar target="_blank"}

- Change **Problem and encoding** to knapsack, the real-valued function vector, and the binary function string. Which rule applies in each case?

## Shuffling a Permutation [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-fisher-yates}

In the traveling salesman problem, the chromosome gives visit order. Can we draw it gene by gene like an integer vector?

No: a city already drawn cannot appear again, so permutation genes are not independent. Drawing each gene independently from 1 to *n* usually repeats cities and fails to produce a permutation, as section -@sec-representacion-permutaciones showed. Uniform initialization still applies to permutations [@talbi2009, p. 195], but needs a different procedure.

The standard shuffle is Fisher and Yates's method [-@fisher1938] in the version of @durstenfeld1964:

1. Start with $(1, 2, \dots, n)$.
2. For $k = n, n - 1, \dots, 2$, draw position $j = 1 + \lfloor u\,k \rfloor$ from 1 to *k*, then swap positions *j* and *k*. Position *k* is now fixed.

Using $n - 1$ random numbers, each of the $n!$ permutations has the same probability.

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-fisher-yates title="Reproducible Example · A Five-City Tour"}
**Data.** A traveling-salesman instance with *n* = 5 cities. Numbers $u$ = 0.087, 0.277, 0.454, and 0.226 have been drawn, one for each *k* from 5 to 2.

**Predict.** What position *j* is selected each time? Which permutation remains?

[Open: shuffle 1 2 3 4 5](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=tsp-perm&n=5&N=6&s=1&ps=1&step=6){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

| *k* | *u* | $j = 1 + \lfloor u\,k \rfloor$ | Swap | Permutation |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| | | | | 1 2 3 4 5 |
| 5 | 0.087 | 1 | positions 1 and 5 | 5 2 3 4 **1** |
| 4 | 0.277 | 2 | positions 2 and 4 | 5 4 3 **2 1** |
| 3 | 0.454 | 2 | positions 2 and 3 | 5 3 **4 2 1** |
| 2 | 0.226 | 1 | positions 1 and 2 | **3 5 4 2 1** |

Bold positions are fixed. The individual is **3 5 4 2 1**, a tour of length 240.8.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the tool here (shuffle 1 2 3 4 5)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=tsp-perm&n=5&N=6&s=1&ps=1&step=6" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: uniform random, traveling salesman"></iframe>
</details>
:::

These are the numbers from example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme): with the same population seed, the tool uses the same random-number sequence on every screen. In this population of six tours, the sixth individual is again 3 5 4 2 1. This is no error: 5 cities allow only $4!/2 = 12$ distinct tours, so drawing six makes a repeat quite likely.

Some shuffles look equivalent but are not. A tempting alternative swaps position *k* with any position from 1 to *n*, rather than 1 to *k*, at each step.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-fisher-yates title="Exercise · A Shuffle That Looks Right"}
With *n* = 3, the procedure “for $k = 1, 2, 3$, swap position *k* with position *j* drawn from 1 to 3” uses three draws with 3 possible values each. (a) How many equally likely draw sequences exist? How many permutations of 3 elements? (b) Can every permutation have the same probability? (c) How many draws does Fisher–Yates use for *n* = 3, and how many sequences exist?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) There are $3^3 = 27$ sequences and $3! = 6$ permutations.

(b) No. Equal probabilities would require each of the 6 permutations to occur in the same number of sequences, but 27 is not divisible by 6. Enumerating the 27 sequences gives permutations 1 3 2, 2 1 3, and 2 3 1 each 5 times, and 1 2 3, 3 1 2, and 3 2 1 each 4 times.

(c) Fisher–Yates uses two draws: *j* from 1 to 3 for *k* = 3 and *j* from 1 to 2 for *k* = 2. This gives $3 \times 2 = 6$ sequences, one per permutation.
</details>
::::

## Diversity and Feasibility of the Initial Population [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad}

How do we measure whether a population is varied? How many individuals describe solutions we can actually use?

Diversity is measured through a **distance** between individuals, normalized in the tool from 0 (identical) to 1 (as different as possible):

- For bit and integer strings, the proportion of differing genes: **Hamming distance** divided by length.
- For tours, the proportion of one tour's edges absent from the other. Thus, the $2n$ chromosomes of one tour have distance 0.
- For real-valued vectors, such as points in $[-5, 5]^2$ from exercise [](#ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme), Euclidean distance divided by the box diagonal, the greatest possible point-to-point distance ($10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.1$ here).

Population summaries include the **mean distance** across pairs, **minimum distance** (0 means duplicate individuals), and number of **distinct individuals**. For uniformly generated individuals, expected mean distance is 0.5 for bits, $1 - 1/m$ for integers, and about 0.37 for two-real-number points.

Duplicates are not unusual. With 64 possible chromosomes and population size 10, the probability that all are distinct is
$$
\frac{64}{64} \times \frac{63}{64} \times \dots \times \frac{55}{64} \approx 0.48,
$$
less than half. This is the birthday paradox: only 23 people are needed to make a shared birthday more likely than no shared birthday [@diaconis1989].

More importantly, a population **uniform over chromosomes is not uniform over feasible solutions**. If half the chromosomes violate constraints, roughly half the initial population will too. We use this knapsack with capacity *W* = 13 throughout the rest of the chapter:

| Item | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Weight $w_i$ | 4 | 3 | 5 | 8 | 4 | 2 |
| Value $v_i$ | 5 | 4 | 9 | 4 | 7 | 4 |

Of $2^6 = 64$ chromosomes, 34 fit (53.1 %). The optimum is **1 0 1 0 1 0**: items 1, 3, and 5, with weight exactly 13 and value 21.

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad title="Reproducible Example · Eight Random Knapsacks"}
**Data.** The table's knapsack and a uniform population of *N* = 8 individuals:

| I1 | I2 | I3 | I4 | I5 | I6 | I7 | I8 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 011011 | 111101 | 100000 | 010010 | 001011 | 100100 | 111110 | 110110 |

**Predict.** How many fit? Which fitting individual is best? Are any two very similar?

[Open: feasibility](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=17){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: diversity](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=18){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

| Individual | Items | Weight | Value | Fits? |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| I1 | 2, 3, 5, 6 | 14 | 24 | No |
| I2 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 | 22 | 26 | No |
| I3 | 1 | 4 | 5 | Yes |
| I4 | 2, 5 | 7 | 11 | Yes |
| I5 | 3, 5, 6 | 11 | 20 | Yes |
| I6 | 1, 4 | 12 | 9 | Yes |
| I7 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | 24 | 29 | No |
| I8 | 1, 2, 4, 5 | 19 | 20 | No |

**4 of 8** fit (50 %), close to the space's 53.1 %. I5 is the best fitting individual, worth 20; the optimum 21 is absent. Mean pairwise distance is **0.55**, near the expected 0.5, and minimum distance is **0.17**: I1 and I5 differ only in item 2, one bit out of six. All 8 are distinct.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the tool here (feasibility)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=17" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: uniform random, knapsack"></iframe>
</details>
:::

Other representations differ much more. In binary-matrix assignment (section -@sec-representacion-matriz), a row has exactly one 1 with probability $3/8$, and all five rows do so with probability $(3/8)^5 \approx 0.0074$: only 243 of 32 768 matrices are feasible assignments. A uniform population of 8 matrices contains any feasible one with probability $1 - (1 - 0.0074)^8 \approx 0.06$. With integer vectors or permutations, every chromosome is a feasible assignment or tour: an advantage of those representations.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad title="Exercise · Distances by Hand"}
Calculate normalized distances among the first three individuals in example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad): I1 = 011011, I2 = 111101, and I3 = 100000. What are the mean and minimum distances of this three-individual population?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

- I1 and I2 differ at bits 1, 4, and 5: $3/6 = 0.5$.
- I1 and I3 differ at bits 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6: $5/6 \approx 0.83$.
- I2 and I3 differ at bits 2, 3, 4, and 6: $4/6 \approx 0.67$.

The mean across three pairs is $(0.5 + 0.83 + 0.67)/3 = 2/3 \approx 0.67$, and the minimum is 0.5.
</details>
::::

::: {.callout-note .en-app title="In the Application · initialization-and-evaluation-ga, “Uniform random”"}
[Explore in initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=uniform&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits){.explorar target="_blank"}

- At the final step, inspect **Diversity and quality of the population**. Click **Draw the population** several times (each draw restarts the sequence: advance to the end or click **Play**). How much do mean distance and feasible count vary?
- Switch to **Assignment · binary matrix** and check how many individuals are valid assignments.
- Switch to **TSP · permutation** with 5 cities and 20 individuals. How many distinct tours appear?
:::

## Seeding with a Heuristic: A Counterexample [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-sembrar}

If another method has already found a reasonable solution, should we include it in the initial population?

It seems sensible and is common in single-solution methods such as local search. Genetic algorithms need more care. Random initialization is usual; heuristics can help, but whether they pay off depends on the problem [@eiben2015, p. 34 and pp. 172–174]. @surry1996 called seeding with known good solutions **inoculation**: it improved average results and shortened search in their industrial problems, but could worsen the best result across runs because the population was less random. Textbooks therefore warn that greedy or local-search initialization can itself cause premature convergence [@talbi2009, p. 193]. Diversity explains why. A good seed mixed with random individuals may gain many selected copies and displace useful variety. If it is not optimal and variation cannot offset that concentration, search can become trapped nearby.

A **greedy heuristic** builds a solution by taking the apparently best choice at each step. For knapsack, sort by decreasing value-to-weight ratio, an idea dating to @dantzig1957, and include each item if it fits. Here the order is 6 (4/2 = 2), 3 (9/5 = 1.8), 5 (7/4 = 1.75), 2, 1, and 4. Items 6, 3, and 5 fit, weighing 11; no others do. The greedy solution is **0 0 1 0 1 1**, worth 20: good, but below the optimum 21.

How quickly can it take over? Suppose only **binary tournament** selection with replacement acts, without crossover, mutation, or an elite: draw two individuals and keep the better (section -@sec-seleccion-torneo). The best solution wins every tournament it enters, so when rare, its copies almost double each generation. If it eventually fills the population, the generations required give **takeover time** [@goldberg1991].

<details>
<summary>**How the tool calculates copies**</summary>

With *K* copies of the best among *N* individuals, a tournament misses it only if both contestants are others, probability $(1 - K/N)^2$. Given the current copy count, the next generation's expected count is
$$
K' = N\left[1 - \left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right)^2\right].
$$

To draw the expansion, the tool repeatedly applies this formula to the preceding step's mean copy count. This is a **deterministic approximation**, omitting sampling fluctuations. The formula gives a one-generation expectation when *K* is known; iterating it this way does not give the exact mean across many small populations. In those populations, the seed may also be lost by chance (section -@sec-seleccion-seleccion-y-diversidad).
</details>

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-sembrar title="Reproducible Example · One Seeded Copy"}
**Data.** The knapsack from section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad and *N* = 10 individuals: 9 uniform random individuals, whose best value is 18, plus one greedy solution, 001011.

**Predict.** Under binary tournament selection without crossover, mutation, or an elite, how many copies does the deterministic approximation estimate after each generation? When does it approach population size?

[Open: one seeded copy](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=seeded&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=10&s=21&ps=2&K=1&step=12){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

| Generation | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Approximate copies | 1 | 1.9 | 3.4 | 5.7 | 8.1 | 9.7 | 10.0 |

The approximation reaches **9.7 copies at generation 5**: almost the entire population would be the greedy solution, value 20 rather than the optimum. This is not the exact mean of many runs. The sole initial copy may, for example, appear in none of ten tournaments, with probability $0.81^{10} \approx 0.122$: about 12 % of runs lose it immediately.

One seeded copy barely changes initial diversity (mean distance is 0.49 in both populations). The curve warns how selection may later concentrate the population around one solution; it does not guarantee that seed's survival or measure crossover and mutation effects.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the tool here (one seeded copy)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=seeded&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=10&s=21&ps=2&K=1&step=12" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: heuristic seeding, knapsack"></iframe>
</details>
:::

Tournament expansion applies to any best individual, seeded or not. With the same copy count and tournament size, rank matters, not the size of its advantage: value 20 beats value 18 in exactly the same tournaments as value 19.99. Seeding risks directing search toward a preselected solution and losing useful variety. This selection-only example does not show that seeding always worsens a complete genetic algorithm.

Seeding is allowed, but should be deliberate. If used, randomize the heuristic to produce different solutions: its main drawback is lost diversity and stagnation [@talbi2009, p. 198]. A uniform random population is the recommended starting point for a first design.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-sembrar title="Exercise · Takeover by Hand"}
(a) For *N* = 10 and one copy, apply the deterministic approximation to check generations 1, 2, and 3 of example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-sembrar). (b) What is the expected count after one generation with 5 seeded copies? (c) Which item must change in the greedy solution to reach the optimum?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) These are approximation values, not exact finite-population means. Generation 1: $10\,[1 - (0.9)^2] = 10 \times 0.19 = 1.9$. Generation 2: $1 - 1.9/10 = 0.81$ and $10\,[1 - 0.81^2] = 10 \times 0.3439 \approx 3.44$. Generation 3: $1 - 0.3439 = 0.6561$ and $10\,[1 - 0.6561^2] \approx 10 \times 0.5695 \approx 5.7$.

(b) $10\,[1 - (0.5)^2] = 7.5$ copies on average: three quarters of the population after one generation. This one-step expectation is exact.

(c) The greedy solution includes items 3, 5, and 6 (001011); the optimum includes 1, 3, and 5 (101010). Change two genes together: remove item 6 and add 1. Changing only one either violates capacity (adding 1 without removing 6 gives weight 15) or loses value (removing 6 leaves 16).
</details>
::::

::: {.callout-note .en-app title="In the Application · initialization-and-evaluation-ga, “Seeding with a heuristic (counterexample)”"}
[Explore in initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=seeded&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits){.explorar target="_blank"}

- Increase **Copies of the heuristic solution (K)** and watch distinct individuals decrease at **Diversity**.
- Switch to **Assignment · integer vector** and **TSP · permutation**. The heuristic differs: assign each task where it would finish earliest, or use nearest neighbor. Does it find the optimum?
- Click **New instance** until the greedy knapsack solution is optimal. Does the copy curve change?
:::

## From Chromosome to Fitness [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-evaluar}

Once the population exists, how does the algorithm know how good each individual is?

To **evaluate** an individual is to turn its chromosome into a number, its **fitness**, that measures how good it is. The objective function assigns each solution a real value describing its quality. Decoding may be needed first to turn the chromosome into that solution [@eiben2015, p. 30; @talbi2009, p. 43]. Fitness is all selection sees: two individuals with equal fitness are equally good to the algorithm, even if they represent very different solutions.

Evaluation has four steps:

1. **Decode** the genotype into the phenotype, the solution it represents (Section -@sec-representacion-genotipo-fenotipo). In the knapsack, each 1 includes its item.
2. Calculate the **objective** for that solution, even if it violates constraints. In the knapsack, this is total value.
3. Measure **constraint violation**: 0 if all constraints hold, and otherwise how far they are violated. In the knapsack, this is excess weight $e = \max(0,\ \text{weight} - W)$.
4. Combine these into **fitness**. For a feasible individual, fitness equals the objective. Otherwise, we must decide how to handle it. Here we use a simple penalty, the tool's default: $F = \text{value} - e$. Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-penalizacion explains how to choose it.

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-evaluar title="Reproducible Example · Evaluating an Overweight Knapsack"}
**Data.** The knapsack from Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad (*W* = 13) and individual I1 = 011011 from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad). An infeasible individual's fitness is $F = \text{value} - e$.

**Predict.** Which items does it contain? What are their total value and weight? What is its fitness? Will it have the highest fitness in the population?

[Open: fitness of I1](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=pipeline&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=4){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: evaluated population](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=pipeline&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=12){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

1. Decode: the ones are at positions 2, 3, 5, and 6, so it contains items 2, 3, 5, and 6.
2. Objective: value $= 4 + 9 + 7 + 4 = 24$.
3. Violation: weight $= 3 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 14 > 13$. It does not fit; excess weight is $e = 1$.
4. Fitness: $F = 24 - 1 = 23$.

This makes **I1 the best individual in the population**, ahead of I5, which fits and has value 20. Selection would favor a solution that cannot be implemented: the penalty is too small.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the Tool Here (fitness of I1)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=pipeline&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=4" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: from genotype to fitness, knapsack"></iframe>
</details>

:::

The objective is not always the best guide. In satisfiability problems, for example, we seek values of logical variables that make every clause in a formula true. The natural objective is 1 if the formula is satisfied and 0 otherwise. It cannot distinguish a solution that fails one clause from one that fails them all. Counting satisfied clauses gives a fitness that can guide the search; many evolutionary algorithms for this problem use this approach [@gottlieb2002; @talbi2009, p. 44].

Fitness need not come from a formula, either. It may come from a simulation, an experiment, or a person's judgment, making each evaluation slow and expensive [@jin2005fitness; @talbi2009, pp. 46–47]. When a person provides fitness, for example by choosing between designs, images, or sounds, this is called **interactive** evolutionary computation [@takagi2001].

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-evaluar title="Exercise · Evaluate by Hand"}
Using the same knapsack and fitness, $F = \text{value} - e$, evaluate I7 = 111110 and I8 = 110110. Do they rank above or below I5 = 001011, whose value is 20?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

I7 contains items 1–5: value $5 + 4 + 9 + 4 + 7 = 29$, weight $4 + 3 + 5 + 8 + 4 = 24$, excess $e = 11$, and $F = 29 - 11 = 18$.

I8 contains items 1, 2, 4, and 5: value $5 + 4 + 4 + 7 = 20$, weight $4 + 3 + 8 + 4 = 19$, excess $e = 6$, and $F = 20 - 6 = 14$.

Both rank below I5 (20). With this penalty, I1 is the problem: it exceeds capacity by only one unit of weight but has a high value.
</details>
::::

[Explore in initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=pipeline&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits){.explorar target="_blank"}

## Minimizing a Cost: From Objective to Fitness [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-objetivo-aptitud}

Return to the assignment problem in Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme: assign 5 tasks to 3 machines that work simultaneously. A machine's load is the sum of its tasks' processing times. The **makespan** is the largest load, the time when the last machine finishes; we want it to be as small as possible. Section -@sec-representacion-entera explains the problem in detail. Can we use makespan directly as fitness?

That depends on how parents are selected. One widely used method is **roulette-wheel selection**, which gives each individual a selection probability proportional to its fitness,
$$
p_i = \frac{F_i}{\sum_j F_j},
$$
as you will see in Section -@sec-seleccion-ruleta. It requires fitness to satisfy two conditions: larger must be better, and values must never be negative. A cost to be minimized fails the first condition. In operations research, changing the sign, $F = -f$, turns minimization into maximization. But that produces negative fitness values, which cannot define a roulette wheel [@goldberg1989, pp. 75–76]. Several transformations preserve the ordering while giving nonnegative fitness:

- $F = C - f$, where *C* is the largest cost in the current population (or in recent generations, or a fixed value; do not confuse it with $C_{\max}$ in Chapter [](#sec-representacion-entera){.capitulo}, the makespan of one individual). @goldberg1989 [p. 76] proposes this transformation. The worst individual receives $F = 0$ and is never selected by the roulette wheel.
- $F = 1/(1 + f)$, always positive if $f \ge 0$.
- **Rank** fitness: order individuals from worst (rank 1) to best (rank *N*), and use rank as *F*. Ties receive the average of the tied ranks. Only the ordering matters, not the values [@talbi2009, p. 206]. This is the idea behind @baker1985's rank selection: it prevents an exceptional individual from taking almost the entire wheel and maintains pressure when fitness values are similar [@mitchell1998, Section 5.4]. Section -@sec-seleccion-otros-mecanismos introduces its variants.

For a maximization problem whose objective can be negative, such as knapsack value after subtracting a penalty, Goldberg proposes adding a constant, $F = \text{value} + C$, where *C* is the absolute value of the worst objective [@goldberg1989, p. 76].

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-objetivo-aptitud title="Reproducible Example · Six Assignments on the Roulette Wheel"}
**Data.** The population from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme), with makespans $f$ = 21, 9, 8, 14, 14, and 14 (individuals I1 through I6).

**Predict.** With $F = C - f$, what is the probability of selecting the best, I3, in one spin? What about rank fitness? What happens to the worst, I1?

[Open: F = C − f](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=objective&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&tr=cmax&step=5){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: F = 1/(1 + f)](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=objective&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&tr=inv&step=5){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: rank](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=objective&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&tr=rank&step=5){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

With $C = 21$, fitness values $C - f$ are 0, 12, 13, 7, 7, and 7, totaling 46. With ranks, the three individuals tied at 14 occupy ranks 2, 3, and 4 and receive their average, 3; the sum is 21.

| Individual | *f* | $C - f$ | *p* | $1/(1+f)$ | *p* | Rank | *p* |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| I1 | 21 | 0 | 0 % | 0.045 | 10.0 % | 1 | 4.8 % |
| I2 | 9 | 12 | 26.1 % | 0.100 | 21.9 % | 5 | 23.8 % |
| I3 | 8 | 13 | **28.3 %** | 0.111 | **24.3 %** | 6 | **28.6 %** |
| I4, I5, I6 | 14 | 7 | 15.2 % | 0.067 | 14.6 % | 3 | 14.3 % |

The three transformations give the same ordering but divide the wheel differently. With $C - f$, the worst individual is never selected, even though it may carry useful genes. With ranks, the best receives $2/(N + 1) = 2/7 \approx 28.6$ % regardless of its advantage over the runner-up. In *N* = 6 spins, the best would be selected an average of 1.70 times with $C - f$, 1.46 with $1/(1 + f)$, and 1.71 with ranks.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the Tool Here (F = C − f)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=objective&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&tr=cmax&step=5" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: objective versus fitness, assignment"></iframe>
</details>

:::

All four transformations, including $F = -f$, preserve the ordering. A tournament configured to prefer lower cost can compare costs directly, without transforming them. Selection that only compares individuals, such as a tournament, would make exactly the same choices with any of these transformations. With roulette-wheel selection, choosing fitness also chooses **selection pressure**: how strongly selection favors better individuals. Too much leads to premature convergence; too little makes search nearly random. We return to this in Chapters [](#sec-seleccion-ruleta-deja-de-distinguir){.capitulo} and [](#sec-experimentos-diversidad){.capitulo}.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-objetivo-aptitud title="Exercise · Adding a Constant"}
Suppose every makespan in Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-objetivo-aptitud) includes an extra 100 time units of setup, the same for every solution: 121, 109, 108, 114, 114, and 114. The problem is unchanged. (a) With $F = 1/(1 + f)$, how many times more likely is the best individual than the worst? Compare this with the original problem, where the best is about 2.4 times more likely than the worst. (b) Do probabilities change with $C - f$? What about ranks?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) The ratio of best to worst fitness is $(1 + 121)/(1 + 108) = 122/109 \approx 1.12$, compared with $22/9 \approx 2.4$ before. Adding a constant, which does not change the problem, almost eliminates selection pressure. Section -@sec-seleccion-ruleta-deja-de-distinguir shows the same effect with roulette-wheel selection.

(b) With $C - f$, *C* becomes 121 and fitness values remain 0, 12, 13, 7, 7, and 7. Nothing changes because only differences matter. Ranks are unchanged too, because the ordering is the same.
</details>
::::

## Handling Constraints with Penalties [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-penalizacion}

In Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-evaluar), an individual that did not fit in the knapsack beat every individual that did. How much should we penalize an infeasible solution?

When an encoding produces solutions that violate constraints, we have several options: reject them, repair them, use a decoder, or preserve feasibility through the operators, as introduced in Section -@sec-representacion-validez and compared in Advanced Section -@sec-representacion-infactibles. We can also keep them in the population with lower fitness. This last approach, **penalization**, is the most widely used [@coello2002; @talbi2009, p. 49]. We add a term that increases with violation:
$$
F = \text{value} - P \quad \text{(maximize)}, \qquad F = f + P \quad \text{(minimize)}.
$$

There are two decisions. First, how should we measure violation? Counting violated constraints does not tell us whether a solution is nearly feasible. @richardson1989 recommended penalizing a **distance to feasibility**, which indicates the effort needed to repair the solution [@talbi2009, p. 50]. In the knapsack, this is excess weight *e*. Second, we must choose the penalty's form and weight:

- **Linear**, $P = \lambda\, e$: each unit of excess costs λ units of value.
- **Quadratic**, $P = (\lambda\, e)^2$: the penalty grows with squared excess. While $\lambda e < 1$, it penalizes less than the linear form; beyond that, increasingly more.

The **weight λ** is the difficult choice. If it is too small, search may end with infeasible solutions. If it is too large, search may converge to feasible but suboptimal solutions [@michalewicz1996b, Section 3.2.6; @talbi2009, p. 50], because all infeasible solutions fall to the bottom, including those close to the boundary. Yet the optimum often lies on the feasible region's boundary when a constraint is active. @schoenauer1996 even proposed searching only along that boundary. For a particular population containing feasible individuals, we can calculate a **critical weight** λ\*: the threshold above which infeasible individuals cannot outperform the best feasible one. They may tie at the threshold; to put all of them strictly below it, choose $\lambda > \lambda^*$. If *B* is the best feasible value, each infeasible individual with value $z_i > B$ and excess $e_i$ falls below it when $z_i - \lambda e_i < B$. Thus, for a linear penalty,
$$
\lambda^* = \max_i \frac{z_i - B}{e_i}.
$$

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-penalizacion title="Reproducible Example · What Should Excess Weight Cost?"}
**Data.** The population from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad). Its four infeasible individuals are:

| Individual | Value $z_i$ | Weight | Excess $e_i$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| I1 = 011011 | 24 | 14 | 1 |
| I2 = 111101 | 26 | 22 | 9 |
| I7 = 111110 | 29 | 24 | 11 |
| I8 = 110110 | 20 | 19 | 6 |

The best feasible individual is I5 = 001011, with *B* = 20.

**Predict.** What is λ\* for the linear penalty? Who is best with λ = 1 and with λ = 5?

[Open: λ = 1](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=penalty&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&pt=linear&l=1&step=5){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: λ = 5](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=penalty&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&pt=linear&l=5&step=5){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: critical weight](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=penalty&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&pt=linear&l=1&step=6){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

| Individual | $(z_i - B)/e_i$ |
|:---:|:---:|
| I1 | $(24 - 20)/1 = 4$ |
| I2 | $(26 - 20)/9 \approx 0.67$ |
| I7 | $(29 - 20)/11 \approx 0.82$ |
| I8 | $(20 - 20)/6 = 0$ |

The critical weight is **λ\* = 4**, set by I1, which has the smallest excess. With λ = 4, I1 and I5 tie at 20. We need λ > 4 to put every infeasible individual in this population below the best feasible one. With λ = 1, I1 wins with $F = 24 - 1 = 23$. With λ = 5, its fitness falls to $24 - 5 = 19$, and **I5**, which fits, wins with $F = 20$. An almost feasible individual with high value requires a large penalty weight; individuals with large violations are pushed aside even by small weights.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the Tool Here (critical weight)</summary>

</details>

:::

Figure -@fig-penalizacion plots the fitness of all eight individuals against λ. Feasible individuals give horizontal lines. Infeasible individuals give descending lines, steeper for larger excesses.

![Fitness of the eight individuals in Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-penalizacion) as a function of weight λ, with the linear penalty. Between λ = 0.5 and λ\* = 4, I1 is best, although it does not fit (at still smaller λ, I7 wins and does not fit either). Above λ\*, I5, which fits, is best. Original figure, generated with `figuras/04-inicializar-evaluar.py` in the book repository.](figuras/04-penalizacion.svg){#fig-penalizacion fig-alt="Line chart. The horizontal axis shows weight lambda from 0 to 5; the vertical axis shows fitness. Four horizontal lines represent individuals that fit: I5 at 20, I4 at 11, I6 at 9, and I3 at 5. Four descending lines represent individuals that do not fit: I1 starts at 24 and falls with slope 1, I2 starts at 26 with slope 9, I7 at 29 with slope 11, and I8 at 20 with slope 6. I2, I7, and I8 fall below I5 before lambda equals 1. I1 crosses I5 at lambda equal to 4, marked by a dashed vertical line."}

[Enlarge Figure](figuras/04-penalizacion.svg){.ampliar-figura target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

<details>
<summary>Show the Figure Data</summary>

| Individual | Fits? | Fitness with λ | λ = 0 | λ = 1 | λ = 4 | λ = 5 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| I1 | No | $24 - \lambda$ | 24 | 23 | 20 | 19 |
| I2 | No | $26 - 9\lambda$ | 26 | 17 | −10 | −19 |
| I3 | Yes | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| I4 | Yes | 11 | 11 | 11 | 11 | 11 |
| I5 | Yes | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 |
| I6 | Yes | 9 | 9 | 9 | 9 | 9 |
| I7 | No | $29 - 11\lambda$ | 29 | 18 | −15 | −26 |
| I8 | No | $20 - 6\lambda$ | 20 | 14 | −4 | −10 |
</details>

λ\* depends on the population, which changes each generation. Hence **dynamic** penalties, whose weight increases with generations [@joines1994], and **adaptive** penalties, which adjust it to search progress. For example, raise it if the best individual has been infeasible throughout recent generations and lower it if the best has always been feasible [@hadjalouane1997; @michalewicz1996b, Section 3.2.4; @talbi2009, pp. 50–51]. Other methods avoid choosing λ. In @deb2000's tournament, a feasible individual always beats an infeasible one. Between feasible individuals, the better objective wins; between infeasible individuals, the smaller violation wins. Also, with λ = 5, I2, I7, and I8 have negative fitness: roulette-wheel selection would require adding a constant, as in Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-objetivo-aptitud.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-penalizacion title="Exercise · The Quadratic Penalty"}
Using the same population and the quadratic penalty, $F = \text{value} - (\lambda\, e)^2$: (a) what is the critical weight? (b) With λ = 3, what is I1's fitness, and who is best? (c) With the linear penalty and λ = 2, who is best?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) I1 falls below I5 if $24 - (\lambda \times 1)^2 < 20$, that is, if $\lambda^2 > 4$: $\lambda^* = \sqrt{4}/1 = 2$. For the other infeasible individuals, $\sqrt{z_i - B}/e_i$ is $\sqrt{6}/9 \approx 0.27$, $\sqrt{9}/11 \approx 0.27$, and 0. The critical weight is **2**: I1 ties with I5 there, and λ > 2 is required to put it strictly below.

(b) $F = 24 - 3^2 = 15$. The other infeasible individuals fall much lower (for example, I2: $26 - 27^2 = -703$). I5 is best, with 20.

(c) With the linear penalty, λ = 2 is below λ\* = 4: I1 has $F = 24 - 2 = 22 > 20$ and remains best.
</details>
::::

::: {.callout-note .en-app title="In the Application · initialization-and-evaluation-ga, “Constraints as a penalty”"}
[Explore in initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=penalty&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits){.explorar target="_blank"}

## The Cost of Evaluation [[Basic]{.largo}[B]{.corto}]{.nivel .basico} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-coste}

So far, we have evaluated one population. What does evaluation cost over an entire run?

In many problems, evaluation consumes most of a metaheuristic's runtime [@jin2005fitness; @talbi2009, p. 47]. In aerodynamic design, for example, evaluating a structure requires a fluid dynamics simulation that may take more than a day, even on a parallel computer [@talbi2009, p. 47]. Selection, crossover, and mutation cost very little by comparison.

A generational genetic algorithm evaluates *N* individuals each generation. With *G* generations plus the initial population, this gives
$$
N\,(G + 1)
$$
evaluations. This number is the algorithm's **budget**. A fair comparison between algorithms counts evaluations, rather than generations or seconds on a particular computer [@eiben2015, pp. 152–153]. A maximum number of evaluations is therefore a common stopping criterion (Section -@sec-reemplazo-cuando-parar).

Many evaluations are repeated. Selection copies good individuals, and mutation leaves many offspring identical to their parent. With mutation probability $1/L$ per gene, the probability of no change is $(1 - 1/L)^L$, approaching $1/e \approx 0.37$ as *L* grows. A **cache**, a table storing chromosomes and their fitness values, avoids evaluating a previously seen individual again: look it up before evaluating [@kratica1999].

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-coste title="Reproducible Example · What a Cache Saves"}
**Data.** The population from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad) (*N* = 8) evolves for *G* = 6 generations with a minimal algorithm: binary tournament and mutation of each gene with probability $1/L$ (1/6 with 6 items), without crossover. Evaluations are counted with and without caching.

**Predict.** What is the budget? How many evaluations do you think caching saves? With that same budget, how many generations could caching allow? Would it save as much with a 12-item knapsack?

[Open: 6 items](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=cost&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&G=6&step=8){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: 12 items](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=cost&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=12&N=8&s=21&ps=5&G=6&step=8){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

The budget is $8 \times (6 + 1) = 56$ evaluations. With caching, the 6-item knapsack needs only **25**, saving 31 (55 %). The same budget of 56 would reach generation 55. In a space of only 64 chromosomes, without crossover, the population soon fills with previously evaluated chromosomes; after generation 24, hardly any new ones appear. This is an extreme case. With 12 items ($2^{12} = 4\,096$ chromosomes), caching requires 40 evaluations, saves 16 (29 %), and reaches generation 9.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the Tool Here (6 items)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=cost&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&G=6&step=8" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: evaluation cost, knapsack"></iframe>
</details>

:::

Caching has conditions. It requires **deterministic** fitness: evaluating the same individual twice must give the same result. We examine this in Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-ruido. It uses memory, one entry per distinct individual. The cache key also matters: in the traveling salesman problem, the $2n$ chromosomes representing the same tour have equal length, so caching by tour would save more than caching by chromosome. Other ways to save evaluations include parallel evaluation and replacing some evaluations with an approximate model, discussed in [Further Reading](#sec-inicializar-evaluar-ampliaciones).

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-coste title="Exercise · Budgets"}
(a) An algorithm with *N* = 50 individuals runs for 100 generations. How many evaluations does it perform? If each is a one-minute simulation, how long does it take? (b) With mutation probability $1/L$ per gene, what is the probability that an offspring has no changes if *L* = 6? What if *L* = 100?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) $50 \times 101 = 5\,050$ evaluations, about 5 050 minutes: more than 84 hours, or three and a half days without stopping.

(b) With *L* = 6, $(5/6)^6 \approx 0.33$. With *L* = 100, $(0.99)^{100} \approx 0.37$. In both cases, about a third of offspring that do not undergo crossover are exact copies of their parent.
</details>
::::

::: {.callout-note .en-app title="In the Application · initialization-and-evaluation-ga, “The cost of evaluating”"}
[Explore in initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=cost&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits){.explorar target="_blank"}

- Advance generation by generation and record how many individuals were already cached. Does the number increase or decrease?
- Change **Generations (G)** and **Problem and encoding**. In which problem does caching save least?
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered #resumen}

- Generate the initial population uniformly at random: bits, integers, and real numbers gene by gene; permutations by Fisher–Yates shuffling. It should be diverse; it need not be good.
- Measure diversity with normalized distances between individuals. A uniform population over chromosomes is not uniform over feasible solutions: it may contain many infeasible individuals.
- Seeding with a heuristic may help, but it can also concentrate search around a few solutions. Protect diversity and check the effect in the full algorithm.
- Evaluation means decoding, calculating the objective, measuring violation, and combining these into fitness. A penalty weight λ should be neither too small, allowing infeasible individuals to win, nor too large.
- For roulette-wheel selection, transform cost into fitness ($C - f$, $1/(1 + f)$, or ranks). These preserve ordering but divide the wheel differently. Measure effort in evaluations, $N\,(G + 1)$. A cache avoids repeated evaluations when fitness is deterministic.

To continue the basic path, go to [“Selecting Parents”](05-seleccion.qmd).

## Covering the Box: Quasi-Random Sequences and Latin Hypercube Sampling [[Advanced]{.largo}[A]{.corto}]{.nivel .avanzado} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-cuasialeatoria}

A uniform population spreads individuals evenly *on average*. Does it do so in each particular population, when there are only eight individuals?

No. With few individuals, chance leaves large gaps in some areas and clusters in others. Divide each axis of the box into *N* equal strips. A random point falls outside a given strip with probability $1 - 1/N$, and *N* points leave it empty with probability $(1 - 1/N)^N$. With *N* = 8, this is 0.34: on average, a third of each axis's strips remain empty. As *N* grows, the probability approaches $1/e \approx 0.37$.

Two families of methods spread the population more evenly [@kazimipour2014; @talbi2009, pp. 194–196]:

- **Quasi-random**, or low-discrepancy, **sequences** [@niederreiter1992] aim for points to spread out, rather than merely drawing independent numbers: new points fill gaps left by earlier ones. In general, they provide more diversity than pseudorandom numbers [@talbi2009, p. 195]. @halton1960's sequence uses the **radical inverse** of *i* in a different prime base for each coordinate (2 and 3 in the plane): write *i* in that base and reverse its digits after the decimal point. In base 2, $i = 1, 2, 3, 4$ gives 0.5, 0.25, 0.75, and 0.125: first the midpoint, then the missing quarters, then the eighths. @sobol1967's sequence uses base 2 for all coordinates, combined differently. Both are deterministic: they always produce the same population. @maaranen2004 used them to generate a genetic algorithm's initial population.
- **Latin hypercube sampling** [@mckay1979] is random. Divide each axis into *N* equal strata; two random permutations decide which stratum each individual occupies on each axis, then sample its position within that stratum. Each stratum of each axis receives exactly one individual, like *N* nonattacking rooks on an $N \times N$ chessboard. Talbi presents it as **parallel diversification**, because all solutions are generated together and independently, without evaluating the objective function [@talbi2009, pp. 195–196].

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-cuasialeatoria title="Reproducible Example · Halton by Hand"}

**Predict.** Which points correspond to $i = 1, 2, 3$ and 4? How many of each axis's 8 strips does Halton occupy? What about the uniform population?

In a genetic algorithm, the advantage is modest and is most noticeable with small populations and continuous problems with few variables. Experimental comparisons appear in @maaranen2004 and @kazimipour2014's review. Latin hypercube sampling does not guarantee good coverage of the plane: all eight points could lie on a diagonal while still occupying every strip. Halton and Sobol, as defined here, always give the same population, so independent runs (Section -@sec-experimentos-replicas) require randomizing them.

## Sequential Diversification [[Advanced]{.largo}[A]{.corto}]{.nivel .avanzado} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-inhibicion}

In the population from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme), I4 = (2, 1, 1, 3, 1) and I6 = (3, 1, 1, 3, 1) differ at only one gene. Can we prevent such similar individuals from entering the population?

In **sequential diversification**, solutions are generated one after another to optimize diversity [@talbi2009, p. 195]. The simplest method is **simple sequential inhibition** (SSI). It comes from spatial statistics, where it generates point patterns whose points cannot be too close together [@diggle1983]. In a genetic algorithm, it works as follows: draw a candidate uniformly at random; accept it only if its distance from every individual already accepted is at least δ. Otherwise, discard it and draw another. Repeat until the population is complete [@talbi2009, p. 195].

By construction, the final population has a minimum distance of at least δ between individuals. The drawback is its relatively high cost and the unknown number of candidates needed [@talbi2009, p. 195]. If δ is too large for the space and population size, *N* sufficiently separated individuals may not fit, and the process may never finish. After 50*N* candidates, the tool accepts subsequent candidates without checking distance. In practice, choose δ somewhat below a uniform population's mean distance. Unlike quasi-random sequences and Latin hypercube sampling, SSI needs only a distance measure, so it works with any representation.

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-inhibicion title="Reproducible Example · Six Separated Assignments"}
**Data.** The assignment problem from Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme, *N* = 6, and δ = 0.6: two individuals must differ at least at 3 of their 5 genes. Candidates appear in the same order as the population from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme): (1, 1, 2, 1, 3), (2, 3, 1, 1, 2), (1, 2, 3, 3, 1), (2, 1, 1, 3, 1), (1, 2, 2, 1, 2), (3, 1, 1, 3, 1)…

**Predict.** Which of these six candidates enter the population? How many candidates do you think will be needed in total?

[Open: the fifth candidate](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=ssi&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&d=0.6&step=5){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: the cost](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=ssi&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&d=0.6&step=11){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

The first four enter: their distances to the nearest previously accepted individual are 0.80, 0.80, and 0.60. The fifth, (1, 2, 2, 1, 2), is **0.40** from I1 (they differ at tasks 2 and 5) and is rejected. The sixth, (3, 1, 1, 3, 1), is **0.20** from the fourth and is also rejected. It takes **11 candidates** to obtain 6 individuals: 5 are rejected. The population's minimum distance increases from 0.20 under uniform initialization to 0.60, and its mean from 0.71 to 0.76.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the Tool Here (the cost)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=ssi&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&d=0.6&step=11" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: sequential diversification, assignment"></iframe>
</details>

:::

Sequential inhibition neither considers quality nor spreads the population evenly over the entire space: it only prevents individuals from being too close.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-inhibicion title="Exercise · Accepted or Rejected?"}
(a) Calculate the distance from the fifth candidate in Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-inhibicion), (1, 2, 2, 1, 2), to each of the four accepted individuals. (b) Would it have been accepted with δ = 0.4? (c) For which δ values would the population be exactly the uniform population from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme)?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) Compared with I1 = (1, 1, 2, 1, 3), tasks 2 and 5 change: $2/5 = 0.4$. Compared with I2 = (2, 3, 1, 1, 2), tasks 1, 2, and 3 change: 0.6. Compared with I3 = (1, 2, 3, 3, 1), tasks 3, 4, and 5 change: 0.6. Compared with I4 = (2, 1, 1, 3, 1), all five change: 1. The nearest distance is 0.4.

(b) Yes: 0.4 ≥ 0.4.

(c) The uniform population consists of the first six candidates, with a minimum distance of 0.20 (between the fourth and sixth). For any δ of 0.20 or less, all six enter and the population is uniform, because the rule is “at least δ.” With δ = 0, sequential inhibition is uniform initialization.
</details>
::::

## Feasible Initialization [[Advanced]{.largo}[A]{.corto}]{.nivel .avanzado} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-factible}

If almost every random chromosome is infeasible under some encodings, can we generate a population that satisfies the constraints directly?

Yes, by changing what we sample. For the **knapsack**, shuffle the items using Fisher–Yates (Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-fisher-yates), then process them in that order, including each if it fits in the remaining capacity. The result is always feasible and full: no further item fits. @chu1998 used this type of initialization in their genetic algorithm for the multidimensional knapsack. For the assignment **binary matrix**, simply draw each task's machine, $j = 1 + \lfloor u\,m \rfloor$, and place a single 1 in that column of its row. This is uniform initialization of the integer vector, written as a matrix. Initial feasibility depends on both representation and method.

Feasible initialization has a price. Filling knapsacks biases the population: solutions with few items never appear, even though they are feasible and may carry valuable genes, and individuals are more similar. With complex constraints, finding even one feasible solution may be as hard as solving the problem. It is then more practical to handle constraints during evaluation with penalties (Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-penalizacion), or with repairs and decoders (Section -@sec-representacion-infactibles). Rejecting infeasible solutions is reasonable only when they occupy a very small part of the search space [@talbi2009, p. 49].

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-factible title="Reproducible Example · Full Knapsacks"}
**Data.** The knapsack from Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad (*W* = 13). For the first individual, the shuffled item order is 2, 4, 3, 5, 1, 6.

**Predict.** Which items enter? What are the knapsack's weight and value? Is it full?

[Open: the first individual](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=feasible&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=9){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: population quality](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=feasible&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&step=20){.abrir target="_blank"}

<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

| Item | Weight | Cumulative weight if included | Fits? |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 2 | 3 | 3 | Yes |
| 4 | 8 | 11 | Yes |
| 3 | 5 | 16 | No |
| 5 | 4 | 15 | No |
| 1 | 4 | 15 | No |
| 6 | 2 | 13 | Yes |

The individual is **0 1 0 1 0 1**: weight 13, exactly the capacity, and value 12. It is full but poor, because item 4 is heavy and has little value. All 8 individuals fit (compared with 4 of 8 under uniform initialization with the same seed), and mean feasible value rises from 11.3 to 14.4. But one individual is duplicated: 7 distinct individuals instead of 8.
</details>

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-factible title="Exercise · Order Decides"}
For the same knapsack: (a) which individual results from shuffled order 3, 5, 1, 2, 6, 4? (b) Can this initialization produce 1 0 0 0 0 0? (c) What about the greedy solution, 0 0 1 0 1 1?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) Include item 3 (weight 5), item 5 (9), and item 1 (13); items 2, 6, and 4 no longer fit. The result is **1 0 1 0 1 0**, the optimum.

(b) No. With only item 1 (weight 4), other items still fit, and the procedure would have included them. It produces only full knapsacks.

(c) Yes. With items 3, 5, and 6, the knapsack weighs 11 and has 2 units left. No remaining item fits (the lightest weighs 3), so it is full. Order 6, 3, 5, 1, 2, 4 produces it, for example.
</details>
::::

## Fitness Landscapes [[Advanced]{.largo}[A]{.corto}]{.nivel .avanzado} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-paisaje}

In some problems, a few changes always lead to the optimum; in others, any search gets stuck. What makes the difference?

Imagine each chromosome at a height equal to its fitness: valleys, peaks, plateaus, and cliffs appear. This is the **fitness landscape**. The idea comes from population genetics: @wright1932 [pp. 357–358] proposed it to study evolution [@talbi2009, p. 104]. Three things define it: representation, the **neighborhood** specifying which chromosomes are reachable through a small change, and the objective function [@stadler2002; @talbi2009, p. 104]. The landscape is therefore not a property of the problem alone: change the representation or neighborhood, and the same problem has a different landscape.

A **local optimum** is a chromosome with no better neighbor. A local search that always moves to the best neighbor ends at the local optimum of its starting **basin**. With many local optima—a **rugged** landscape—different starting points lead to different optima and rarely to the global one [@kauffman1987]. A genetic algorithm moves an entire population through the landscape, and crossover can jump between basins. Yet landscape structure still affects difficulty; this is why a diverse initial population starts in many basins at once.

To summarize landscape structure without plotting it, @jones1995 proposed **fitness–distance correlation** (FDC): the correlation between many chromosomes' fitness and their distance to the nearest global optimum [@talbi2009, pp. 114–115]. For minimization, a strong positive correlation indicates a relatively easy problem (fitness improves toward the optimum); a strong negative correlation indicates deception; a value near zero means fitness provides little guidance. Its major limitation is the need to know the optimum, which is unrealistic for many problems [@talbi2009, p. 115]. @malan2013 review other landscape measures, such as fitness autocorrelation along a random walk, that do not require it.

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-paisaje title="Reproducible Example · Moving Through Neighbors"}
**Data.** The assignment problem from Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-uniforme and its one-gene neighborhood: two assignments are neighbors if moving one task to another machine turns one into the other. Local search starts at I1 = (1, 1, 2, 1, 3), with makespan 21, and moves to the best neighbor at each step. Ties are broken by task order, then machine order within each task.

**Predict.** How many neighbors does each assignment have? How many improve on I1? Will local search reach the optimum, 5?

[Open: I1's neighbors](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=landscape&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&step=1){.abrir target="_blank"}
[Open: local search](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=landscape&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&step=2){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

Each task can move to two other machines: $5 \times 2 = 10$ neighbors. Of I1's neighbors, **6 are better**; the best moves task 2 to machine 2, reducing makespan to 12. Local search proceeds as follows:

| Step | Assignment | Move | Makespan |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | (1, 1, 2, 1, 3) | | 21 |
| 1 | (1, 2, 2, 1, 3) | task 2 to machine 2 | 12 |
| 2 | (1, 2, 2, 3, 3) | task 4 to machine 3 | 11 |
| 3 | (1, 2, 1, 3, 3) | task 3 to machine 1 | **7** |

It stops at a **local optimum**, makespan 7, without reaching the optimum, 5. Tie-breaking matters too: at step 3, moving task 3 to machine 3 also gives 7, and from there search would reach the optimum. Starting from the population's six individuals gives 5 distinct local optima; only one search reaches the global optimum. The entire space of 243 assignments contains 25 local optima, only one global. Fitness–distance correlation over 500 random assignments is 0.39: fitness offers some guidance, but not much.
</details>

<summary>Show the Tool Here (local search)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=landscape&lang=en&enc=assignment-int&n=5&m=3&N=6&s=1&ps=1&step=2" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: fitness landscape, assignment"></iframe>

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-paisaje title="Exercise · Is It a Local Optimum?"}
Check that assignment (1, 2, 1, 3, 3), where the search in Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-paisaje) ends, is a local optimum. (a) Calculate its loads. (b) Which task would need to move to reduce makespan below 7? Is moving one enough? (c) How many neighbors also have makespan 7?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

(a) Machine 1 handles tasks 1 and 3: $5 + 2 = 7$. Machine 2 handles task 2: 2. Machine 3 handles tasks 4 and 5: $1 + 5 = 6$. Makespan is 7.

(b) To get below 7, we must reduce machine 1's load by moving task 1 or 3. Moving task 1 to machine 2 gives $2 + 5 = 7$; moving it to machine 3 gives $6 + 8 = 14$. Moving task 3 to machine 2 gives $2 + 9 = 11$; moving it to machine 3 gives $6 + 1 = 7$. No single-task move gets below 7, so it is a local optimum. Reaching the optimum, (1, 2, 3, 3, 2), requires moving two tasks: task 3 to machine 3 and task 5 to machine 2.

(c) Four neighbors also have makespan 7: task 1 to machine 2, task 3 to machine 3, task 4 to machine 2, and task 5 to machine 2. This is a **plateau**: local search that accepts only improving neighbors stops there.
</details>
::::

## Noisy Fitness [[Advanced]{.largo}[A]{.corto}]{.nivel .avanzado} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-ruido}

What if evaluating the same individual twice produces different numbers?

In many real problems, data contain **noise**. Fitness may come from a stochastic simulator or a sensor, or data may be uncertain: variable processing times in scheduling or random demands along a route, for example [@talbi2009, p. 15]. We can write
$$
\tilde F(x) = f(x) + \varepsilon,
$$
where ε is noise, often assumed normal with mean 0 and standard deviation σ. In practice, fitness is approximated by averaging several evaluations [@talbi2009, p. 15].

With noise, selection compares values that differ from true fitness. If the true difference Δ between two individuals is small relative to σ, their apparent ordering is almost a coin toss. The mean of *R* evaluations has the same expected value and standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{R}$. The difference between two individuals' means therefore has standard deviation $\sigma\sqrt{2/R}$, and the probability of ordering them incorrectly is
$$
\Phi\!\left(-\frac{\Delta\sqrt{R}}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}\right),
$$
where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Reevaluation costs: *N* individuals evaluated *R* times require $N \times R$ evaluations per generation, and halving the error requires four times as many.

::: {.callout-tip .ejemplo #ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-ruido title="Reproducible Example · Two Individuals Mistaken for Each Other"}
**Data.** A uniform population of 8 points on the Himmelblau function, to be minimized. The two best are I1, with true fitness 52.555, and I7, with 91.112: a difference Δ ≈ 38.56. Each evaluation adds normal noise with σ = 30. Compare one evaluation per individual with the mean of *R* = 5.

**Predict.** What is the probability of ordering I1 and I7 incorrectly with one evaluation? What about the mean of 5? How many evaluations does each option require?

[Open: the cost](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=noise&lang=en&enc=function-real&fn=himmelblau&N=8&s=1&ps=1&sg=30&R=5&step=5){.abrir target="_blank"}

<details>
<summary>**Show the Result**</summary>

With one evaluation, $\Delta/(\sigma\sqrt 2) = 38.56/42.43 \approx 0.91$ and $\Phi(-0.91) \approx$ **18.2 %**. With the mean of 5, multiply the argument by $\sqrt 5$: $\Phi(-2.03) \approx$ **2.1 %**. The price is 40 evaluations rather than 8. To get below 5 %, 4 evaluations per individual suffice. In this population, incorrectly ordered pairs fall from 5 to 2 out of 28.
</details>

<details class="incrustada">
<summary>Show the Tool Here (the cost)</summary>
<iframe data-external="1" src="https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=noise&lang=en&enc=function-real&fn=himmelblau&N=8&s=1&ps=1&sg=30&R=5&step=5" loading="lazy" title="initialization-and-evaluation-ga: noisy fitness, function"></iframe>
</details>

:::

Noise changes other decisions too. The cache from Section -@sec-inicializar-evaluar-coste no longer works as described: it would preserve a lucky evaluation forever. Elitism (Section -@sec-reemplazo-elitismo) can retain an individual that merely appeared good. The final solution should be evaluated several times before accepting it. Cheaper alternatives to reevaluating everyone include increasing population size, which implicitly averages noise, or reevaluating only individuals involved in close comparisons. @jin2005 review these techniques.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-ruido title="Exercise · How Many Evaluations?"}
With the data from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-ruido) (Δ = 38.56, σ = 30), how many evaluations per individual make the probability of ordering I1 and I7 incorrectly less than 5 %? Use $\Phi(-1.645) = 0.05$.

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

We need $\Delta\sqrt{R}/(\sigma\sqrt 2) \ge 1.645$, or $0.909\,\sqrt R \ge 1.645$, $\sqrt R \ge 1.81$, and $R \ge 3.27$. Since *R* is an integer, **R = 4**. With *N* = 8, that means 32 evaluations per generation instead of 8.
</details>
::::

::: {.callout-note .en-app title="In the Application · initialization-and-evaluation-ga, “Noisy fitness”"}
[Explore in initialization-and-evaluation-ga](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=noise&lang=en&enc=function-real){.explorar target="_blank"}

- Change **Noise (σ)** and **Evaluations per individual (R)**, and watch how many pairs are ordered incorrectly.
- Switch to **TSP · permutation**. What σ makes the apparent best individual differ from the true best?

## Further Reading [[Further reading]{.largo}[+]{.corto}]{.nivel .saber-mas} {#sec-inicializar-evaluar-ampliaciones}

**Approximate fitness.** When an evaluation takes hours, some evaluations can be replaced with a **meta-model**: a cheap function approximating the objective from a sample of previously evaluated solutions. This is also called a surrogate model or approximate fitness. Neural networks, response surfaces, kriging, and Gaussian processes are common meta-models [@jin2005fitness; @jin2011; @talbi2009, pp. 47–48]. The tradeoff is familiar: exact, expensive evaluation versus cheap evaluation with error; the two can be alternated [@talbi2009, p. 48]. A typical use is **preselection**: the meta-model identifies promising candidates from a larger set, and only those are evaluated exactly. In the tool's “[Approximate fitness](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=surrogate&lang=en&enc=function-real&fn=himmelblau&N=8&s=1&ps=1&sm=idw&step=4){target="_blank"}” view, an inverse-distance-weighting meta-model built from the initial population's 8 individuals ranks 8 new candidates rather poorly (rank correlation 0.26). Yet evaluating only its estimated best 4 saves 4 evaluations and includes the true best candidate.

**Multiple objectives.** Many real problems have conflicting objectives: a more valuable knapsack weighs more. There is then no single solution better than all others, but a set of tradeoffs. One solution **dominates** another if it is no worse in any objective and better in at least one. Solutions dominated by no other solution in the search space are **Pareto optima** [@deb2001; @talbi2009, p. 311]. Within a population, “nondominated” means only that no other member of that population dominates it. There are two ways to evaluate. A **weighted sum** normalizes and combines objectives using weights, turning the problem into a single-objective problem. Its drawback is that it finds only **supported** solutions: no choice of weights selects solutions in a nonconvex part of the front [@talbi2009, pp. 324–325]. Alternatively, fitness can be assigned by dominance. Nondominated individuals form the first front; remove them, and the remaining nondominated individuals form the second, and so on. In “[Several objectives](https://josemagalan.github.io/initialization-and-evaluation-ga/#item=multi&lang=en&enc=knapsack-bits&n=6&N=8&s=21&ps=5&w=0.5&step=3){target="_blank"}”, using the population from Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad) without the knapsack's capacity constraint (maximize value and minimize weight), the first front has 6 individuals, and no choice of weights selects 2 of them.

:::: {.callout-note .ejercicio #ejercicio-inicializar-evaluar-ampliaciones title="Exercise · Who Dominates Whom?"}
Without the capacity constraint, each individual in Example [](#ejemplo-inicializar-evaluar-diversidad) has two objectives: value, to be maximized, and weight, to be minimized. Which individuals are dominated, and by whom?

<details>
<summary>**Show the Solution**</summary>

The pairs (value; weight) are I1 (24; 14), I2 (26; 22), I3 (5; 4), I4 (11; 7), I5 (20; 11), I6 (9; 12), I7 (29; 24), and I8 (20; 19). I6 is dominated by I4 (higher value and lower weight) and by I5. I8 is dominated by I5 (equal value and lower weight) and by I1. The other six form the first front.
</details>
::::

For the history of multiobjective genetic algorithms, from early methods to more recent ones, and further reading, see “[Multiple Objectives](#fuera-objetivos)” in Section -@sec-recapitulacion-fuera.

**A population diverse by construction.** Generating the initial population can itself be an optimization problem: choose *N* solutions that maximize a diversity measure, such as the smallest distance between any pair. This can be as difficult as the original problem, so approximate methods are used. For example, generate part of the population at random, then add solutions one at a time, choosing those farthest from the individuals already present [@talbi2009, pp. 194, 197–198].

**Relative fitness.** Some problems have no absolute value to measure. In a game, for example, strategy A may beat B, B beat C, and C beat A. Fitness then comes from comparing individuals, through ranks or competitions. This is enough for population algorithms, because selection needs only to know who is better [@talbi2009, p. 47].

**More to read.** @kazimipour2014 review population initialization techniques in evolutionary algorithms; @coello2002 reviews constraint-handling methods.
